title: Do We Really Need Permutations? Impact of Model Width on Linear Mode Connectivity
claim: Without any alignment procedure, increasing model capacity alone removes the performance barrier between two independently trained models.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared axes, one line per width multiplier
description: A single row of four line plots, one per model and dataset pair: MLP on MNIST, MLP on FMNIST, VGG-11 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10. In each plot the x-axis is the interpolation coefficient lambda from 0 to 1, and the y-axis is test accuracy from 50 to 100. Each plot has several curves with error bars, coloured by width multiplier on a purple-to-green scale. The legend sits in the lower left of each plot. The multipliers run from x0.125 to x16 for the MLPs and VGG, and from x1 to x32 for ResNet-20. Narrow models (dark purple) show a deep V-shaped accuracy dip at lambda=0.5, in some cases falling below the 50 axis limit. Wider models (green) have a shallow dip and stay close to the endpoint accuracy. The eye goes first to the dip at the centre of each plot and to how it shrinks as the colours move from purple to green.
caption: Test accuracies of merged models without permutations for different values of the interpolation coefficient λ. Even in the absence of permutations, increasing the width multiplier enables the merged models to reach accuracy comparable to the original models (corresponding to λ = 0 and 1).
abstract: Recently, Ainsworth et al. empirically demonstrated that, given two independently trained models, applying a parameter permutation that preserves the input-output behavior allows the two models to be connected by a low-loss linear path. When such a path exists, the models are said to achieve linear mode connectivity (LMC). Prior studies, including Ainsworth et al.(2023), have reported that achieving LMC requires not only an appropriate permutation search but also sufficiently wide models (e.g., a 32 $\times$ width multiplier for ResNet-20). This is broadly believed to be because increasing the model width ensures a large enough space of candidate permutations, increasing the chance of finding one that yields LMC. In this work, we empirically demonstrate that, even without any permutations, simply widening the models is sufficient for achieving LMC when using a suitable softmax temperature calibration. We further explain why this phenomenon arises by analyzing intermediate layer outputs. Specifically, we introduce layerwise exponentially weighted connectivity (LEWC), which states that the output of each layer of the merged model can be represented as an exponentially weighted sum of the outputs of the corresponding layers of the original models. Consequently the merged model's output matches that of an ensemble of the original models, facilitating LMC. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to show that widening the model not only facilitates nonlinear mode connectivity, as suggested in prior research, but also significantly increases the possibility of achieving linear mode connectivity.
